tags.description: The work the machine could not finish on its own: dead-lettered notifications, and the queue somebody is looking at. Platform-scoped, redacted, and audited — an operations tool is read on shared screens, so it shows statuses rather than customers’ mail.

tags.name: webhooks
tags.description: Provider callbacks. The authoritative signal that money moved, verified over the exact bytes sent.

tags.name: analytics
tags.description: What an organiser’s events actually did: tickets gone, seats left, people admitted, refunds and disputes outstanding, and the money behind all of it. Every figure is counted from the record it belongs to — money from the append-only ledger, inventory from the seats themselves — and a measurement this system does not record is named as missing rather than estimated.

tags.name: finance
tags.description: Money leaving: what an organiser is owed, what is held against it, and the payouts, transfers and disputes that move it. Every figure is derived from the append-only ledger rather than read off a column, and a reversal posts compensating entries rather than editing history.

tags.name: refunds
tags.description: Giving money back: requesting, approving, submitting and withdrawing. Every amount is computed from the order, every step is audited, and the provider is called with no transaction open — a refund is the one commerce action where every failure mode costs somebody money.

tags.name: privacy
tags.description: Redacting a person’s personal data, and the record of having done it. Organisation-scoped and never platform-wide: one request names one subject inside one organisation. Redaction is irreversible — no reversal path, original value, encrypted copy or recoverable mapping is stored — so every command here needs the narrow `privacy:redact` capability, a step-up no older than two minutes, and a single-use confirmation the server issued. Nothing on this surface returns a value that was or will be redacted: a request is described by counts and categories, and the subject by an opaque id.

post.description: Exchange email and password for a session, returned both as a cookie and as a bearer token carrying the same secret. get.description:
Every redaction request raised inside this organisation, newest first, with its state, the reason code it was raised under, what the hold evaluation concluded and how much there was to redact. Requires `privacy:redact`, which is granted to the organisation owner alone: reading who has asked to be removed is part of the same decision as removing them. Filterable by state and by subject id — by id and never by address, because searching by e-mail would make this endpoint a way to confirm whether a named person is in the system, which is the question a redaction exists to stop answering. Carries no value that was or will be redacted, and no organisation but the caller’s own: the organisation is read from the path and the capability is asserted against it, so another tenant’s identifier answers 404 rather than 403.

Requires the `privacy:redact` capability.

post.description:
Opens a request to redact one person’s personal data inside this organisation, and returns a single-use confirmation phrase that must be typed back to execute it. Nothing is redacted here. Requires `privacy:redact` and a `PRIVACY_ERASURE` step-up no older than two minutes, both asserted against the organisation in the path. The body carries a subject id and a reason code and nothing else: the organisation, the idempotency key, the confirmation phrase, the policy revision and the hold decision are all produced on the server, because a request body that could carry them would be a request body that could lie about them. Refuses with 409 when a legal hold, a fraud investigation or an open operational process — a pending ticket transfer, a refund still moving, an unspent admission — still needs the data, and records the refusal as immutable evidence. The confirmation phrase appears in this response and nowhere else; only its digest is stored.

Requires the `privacy:redact` capability.

Requires a recent step-up authentication: see `POST /v1/auth/step-up`.

A request belonging to another organisation and a request that does not exist answer the same 404, deliberately: a caller must not be able to learn that an identifier is real by the shape of the refusal. Describes the subject by opaque id and the scope by counts — never by a name, an address, or the value of any field, before or after redaction.

post.description:
The irreversible one. Accepts the confirmation phrase the server issued when the request was raised, re-evaluates every hold at the moment of execution rather than trusting the evaluation made when the request was opened, and then replaces the subject’s personal fields with placeholders derived from each row’s own id. Financial facts are untouched: amounts, currency, tax, order state, refund state, payout state, ledger entries and ticket status all survive unchanged, because erasure here is redaction of identity rather than deletion of rows. Requires `privacy:redact` and a fresh `PRIVACY_ERASURE` step-up. Idempotent: confirming an already-completed request returns the original outcome and writes nothing. There is no reversal path, no original value, no encrypted copy and no recoverable mapping stored anywhere — once this returns 200, the values are gone.

Requires the `privacy:redact` capability.

Requires a recent step-up authentication: see `POST /v1/auth/step-up`.

Requires the `privacy:redact` capability.

get.description:
Every recorded step of one request, oldest first: raised, refused, confirmed, completed or stopped safely, each with the actor, the hold decision, the policy revision and a closed-vocabulary reason code. These rows are append-only at the database — `desi_privacy_audit_event_immutable` refuses both `UPDATE` and `DELETE` — so a timeline read here is the same timeline that was written. Every field is an opaque id, an enum, a code, a count or a timestamp: there is no before-value, no after-value and no message, which is what makes this safe to read while investigating an incident about somebody who has already been redacted. Requires `privacy:redact` on the organisation in the path.

sessionCookie.description: The session cookie set by `POST /v1/auth/login`. A state-changing request must also echo the `__Host-desi_csrf` cookie in the `x-desi-csrf` header and arrive from an expected origin. On a deployment served over plain HTTP the cookies lose their `__Host-` prefix.

bearerAuth.description: The same session secret `POST /v1/auth/login` returns as `token`, presented as a bearer token instead of a cookie. Opaque, not a JWT: it is the key to a session row, so revoking the session revokes the token.
